content.title: About
content.content: Corn is a cereal grain cultivated worldwide. Cooked corn from a restaurant is usually served on the cob or as kernels boiled or steamed. It has a mildly sweet flavor, tender texture, and provides carbohydrates, fiber, and several vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn was domesticated over 9,000 years ago in Mexico.
There are more than 300 varieties of corn, differing in color and kernel size.
Corn is a staple food in many countries, including Mexico, the United States, and several African nations.
Corn on the cob is featured in traditional dishes such as Mexican elote or Russian roasted corn.
Corn contains antioxidants like lutein and zeaxanthin that support eye health.

items.title: Rich in carbohydrates
items.content: Cooked corn provides a quick source of energy thanks to its complex carbohydrate content.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Corn supplies thiamine (B1), niacin (B3) and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It provides magnesium, phosphorus and potassium, supporting muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Eye‑supporting antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin help protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to corn.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Corn can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: GMO concerns
items.content: Much of the commercial corn supply is genetically modified; choose organic options if preferred.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Corn can be enjoyed on the cob, added to salads, soups, side dishes, or used as flour and grits. It pairs well with butter, salt, spices, cheese, and sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked corn in the refrigerator in an airtight container for 3‑4 days. Frozen corn can be kept for up to 6 months.

content.title: About
content.content: An oatmeal muffin is a baked treat that incorporates whole rolled oats, whole grains, and often nuts or dried fruit. It combines the soft, slightly sweet texture of a muffin with the nutritional benefits of oats, making it a convenient snack or breakfast option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oatmeal muffins are frequently made gluten‑free by using certified gluten‑free oats.
The oats add beta‑glucans, soluble fibers known for heart‑health benefits.
Recipes often include spices such as cinnamon, ginger, and nutmeg, enhancing flavor and antioxidant content.
Portion‑controlled packaging makes them popular in school lunchboxes.
Protein‑boosted versions add whey or plant protein powder for extra muscle‑building benefits.

items.title: Rich in beta‑glucans
items.content: Beta‑glucans help lower cholesterol and support immune function.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Oats provide slow‑release energy, keeping you feeling full longer.

items.title: Contains plant protein
items.content: When combined with nuts or seeds, the muffin supplies essential amino acids.

items.title: High in B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B5, and folate aid metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Provides iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are important for blood formation and muscle function.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: If made with regular wheat flour, the product is unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweetened versions may contain added sugars, which can be problematic for diabetics.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Muffins are relatively calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Added oils
items.content: Excessive oil can increase saturated fat levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy an oatmeal muffin as a standalone snack, split it and spread cottage cheese, yogurt, or nut butter. It’s easy to take on the go and pairs well with tea or coffee.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 5 days. For longer shelf life keep refrigerated (up to 2 weeks) or freeze (up to 3 months). Discard if mold or off‑odors appear.
